newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Ciba Speciality launches spinoff.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Ciba Speciality launches spinoff.

text.p: Ciba Specialty Chemicals Holding Inc launched one of world's biggest spin-offs on Tuesday by indicating its global public offering of stock would be priced between 72 and 86 Swiss francs per registered share.

The range, in line with to slightly below what analysts expected, marks the likely price at which new investors can buy shares after current Novartis shareholders get the right to take up stock in the special chemicals company which it is divesting.
Analysts expected the offer to meet good demand.
"Fundamentally it is very interesting," Union Bancaire Privee's Romain Pasche said, adding that Ciba's decent mid-term outlook as a pure specialty chemicals play should lure investors.
Zurich Cantonal Bank said it saw shares opening around 80 francs but Bank Sarasin's Gilbert Puder was more bullish.
"Even the higher level (of 86 francs) seems rather cheap. I think it is worth well up to 95 francs," he said, forecasting shares would easily surpass 100 francs within three months.

"It is much cheaper than comparative U.S. or European stocks in specialty chemicals," he said. "Even if you take the higher level of 86 francs, the enterprise value (market capitalisation plus net debt) is less than 90 percent of the sales figures, which is rather cheap."
The company's broad equity base of some four times its net debt also gives it room to take over other companies without a capital increase on taking on more debt, Puder added.

He hailed Ciba's method of insisting that top managers invest a year's pay in a stock plan and awarding large cash bonuses to those who meet financial targets as a way to boost profitability and keep the share price moving up.

"These are people who have worked together for several years and succeeded in having decent results even in periods of difficult business cycles and in periods when the Swiss franc has been very strong," he added.
Puder said 86 francs represented only around 12 times his estimated 1998 earnings of seven francs per share.
Ciba is a giant in its own right, with 1996 sales of more than 6.7 billion Swiss francs ($4.5 billion) from additives, consumer care chemicals, polymers, pigments and textile dyes.

It is the world's market leader in additives, whiteners, certain polymers and pigments. It is second in textile dyes to Clariant AG, spun off by Sandoz AG before it merged with Ciba-Geigy AG to form Novartis last year.
Clariant is buying Hoechst AG's specialty chemicals business to become global market leader in the high-end sector.

Ciba officials said at least 300 million francs worth of shares would be included in the public offering. Share allocation and pricing will be announced on March 13. The stock will trade in Switzerland and on SEAQ International in London.

The transaction consists of a one-for-one rights issue to Novartis shareholders and a rights bid. Holders of more than 72 million Novartis shares get the right to buy one Ciba share for each Novartis share at a subscription price of 10 francs per share.
Novartis shareholders can exercise their rights, sell them at market prices or sell the rights to a bank syndicate at a rights bid price to be announced early on March 11.
Rights will trade on the Swiss Exchange from February 26 through March 11 and be reflected in the blue-chip Swiss Market Index, the first time that rights have made up a major Swiss index component.
Shares obtained in the rights bid will be offered to new investors. Ciba will not issue any new shares for the deal.
Credit Suisse First Boston and Union Bank of Switzerland are joint global co-ordinators of the transaction.

Ciba said it had a 1996 first-half net loss of 615 million francs, compared with a profit of 303 million in the same period of 1995. The loss reflected 1.1 billion francs in restructuring and one-off charges in 1996.
Chairman Rolf Meyer told reporters Ciba expected a marginal increase in operating profits before restructuring and one-time charges for the full year 1996 but he gave no figures.
The company said it expected further restructuring charges of between 250 million and 300 million francs for 1997.
"We will follow a flexible dividend policy and (have) a payout ratio of some 20 to 25 percent," Meyer said.
Company officials said they expected growth to be fuelled internally but added they would look at any attractive opportunities in the market. ($ = 1.483 Swiss Francs)
